findings.evidence: Reader has On anginne gescēop God heofonan and eorðan. Vocabulary gives an-ginn (ongin) with beginning among the senses.
findings.conclusion: Cook directly establishes the noun/spelling and identifies an-/on- lexical variants. The entry marks neither consonant quality nor primary stress. A hyphen is not a phonetic transcription.

Wright explicitly marks root stress in the on- noun and states that this noun was formed directly from the corresponding verb. This is evidence for that selected on- form, not an automatic pronunciation identity for every lexical variant.

Wright explicitly calls an- the stressed form of the preposition on and includes anginn as an example. This prevents transferring the primary root stress of ongínn to anginn without qualification. The book itself presents stress-related an-/on- evidence, not one undifferentiated rule.

The noun has no later-stress marker. Sweet says unmarked hyphenated words generally stress their first syllable and explicitly marks later stress (e.g. be·cuman). Applying the stated convention supports first-syllable stress here. That is compatible with Wright§568; it differs from simply applying Wright’s ongínn accentuation.
The noun entry provides no usable contrast distinguishing hard g from palatal g; other entries such as and-giet also have undotted g. No hard-g conclusion can be drawn from lack of a dot.

These pages contain no anginn example and do not prescribe its root stress. The earlier course’s stressed-stem wording is not independent source authority and does not itself specify primary versus secondary stress.

consonant_result.limit: Fulk’s marked related verbs plus Wright’s explicit derivational statement may inform a declared analytical inference, but this worker has not found an inspected noun-specific phonetic witness establishing the consonant sequence. stress_result.anginn: Wright§568 treats an- as stressed and supplies anginn; Sweet’s stated marking convention also supports first-syllable stress.
stress_result.limit: Lexical identity does not by itself collapse these stress patterns. No assertion of a universal primary-root-stress pronunciation of Cook anginne is certified.
